lessons.title: Your changing fuel needs
body: Pregnancy is not simply “eating for two.” Your body is growing the placenta, increasing its blood supply, supporting the baby’s growth, and adapting its heart, lungs, digestion, and metabolism. Plasma volume rises by more than 40% during pregnancy, while cardiac output and oxygen demand rise too. That helps explain why you may feel warmer, tired faster, or slightly out of breath doing activities that once felt easy.

The increase in energy needs is real, but it is usually gradual rather than dramatic. During the earliest weeks, your body may not need much more energy at all. In later pregnancy, especially when the baby grows more quickly, you may notice that hunger changes. Some days you may want extra food; on other days nausea, heartburn, or tiredness may make larger meals difficult.

A useful way to understand this is to think about nutrient density rather than simply more food. Nutrient-dense foods provide protein, fibre, vitamins, minerals, and healthy fats in a relatively small amount of food. For example, yoghurt and fruit, eggs on toast, beans in a soup, or a handful of nuts can offer more sustained nutrition than a large snack that is mostly sugar.

Pregnancy can also bring mixed feelings about eating. You might hear comments from relatives, see conflicting advice online, or feel pressure to eat “perfectly.” Natal IQ should counter this with a calmer message: one meal does not define a pregnancy. Eating patterns over time matter more than a single day, craving, or takeaway.
keyPoints: More blood and higher oxygen demand can make tiredness and breathlessness feel more noticeable.
Hunger and appetite may vary across trimesters and even from day to day.
Pregnancy nutrition is not about rigid perfection or doubling every meal.
A balanced pattern over time is more useful than judging individual foods.
If eating feels persistently difficult because of nausea, vomiting, anxiety, or another concern, it is appropriate to raise it with a midwife or doctor.
Gentle takeaway: Your body is doing demanding work. Regular meals, flexible expectations, and food choices that work for you are a better foundation than the pressure to “eat perfectly.”

lessons.title: Protein power
body: Protein helps build and repair tissue throughout the body. During pregnancy, it supports the growth of the baby, placenta, uterus, and breast tissue, while also helping maintain the mother’s own muscles, blood, skin, and immune function. Research using US dietary data describes the recommended dietary allowance as about 46 g per day in the first trimester and 71 g per day in the second and third trimesters.

That increase can sound intimidating, but it does not mean every meal needs to be built around a large portion of meat. Protein is found across many foods: eggs, yoghurt, cheese, fish, poultry, meat, beans, lentils, chickpeas, tofu, tempeh, nuts, seeds, and fortified plant-based products. A person who is vegetarian, vegan, has food allergies, or dislikes certain foods can still discuss appropriate ways to meet nutritional needs with a healthcare professional.

Instead of treating protein as a number to obsess over, Natal IQ can teach the “protein anchor” idea. This simply means including a protein-containing food in meals and many snacks. For example, toast can become toast with egg or nut butter; fruit can be paired with yoghurt; soup can contain lentils or beans; a bowl of cereal can be served with milk or a fortified alternative.

Protein can also help meals feel more satisfying. When paired with fibre-rich carbohydrates and healthy fats, it can contribute to steadier energy levels. That may be particularly useful on long days, when appetite is unpredictable, or when pregnancy tiredness makes cooking feel difficult.

The research also found that approximately one in eight women in the second and third trimester did not meet the estimated average requirement for protein, showing that this is a realistic gap rather than a niche issue. The purpose of this lesson is not to worry users — it is to help them recognise simple ways to make meals more complete.
keyPoints: Protein needs rise as pregnancy progresses, especially after the first trimester.
Protein comes from animal and plant foods; no single diet pattern is the only way to eat well.
Spreading protein across the day can feel easier than concentrating it in one meal.
Low appetite, nausea, dietary restrictions, and limited time can all make food planning harder.
A healthcare professional can give individual advice if there are concerns about diet, weight change, nausea, anaemia, diabetes, or an eating disorder.
sources: Murphy MM, et al. “Adequacy and Sources of Protein Intake among Pregnant Women in the United States, NHANES 2003–2012.” Nutrients (2021). Used for pregnancy protein requirements and protein-source data.
NHS. “Vegetarian or vegan and pregnant.” Used for plant-based protein, fortified foods, and pregnancy nutrition considerations.
Jouanne M, et al. “Nutrient Requirements during Pregnancy and Lactation.” Used for broader pregnancy-nutrition context.

extras.heading: Example: a flexible protein day
items: Breakfast: porridge made with milk, or toast with egg.
Snack: yoghurt, nuts, cheese, hummus, or soy yoghurt.
Lunch: lentil soup, bean salad, chicken wrap, tofu stir-fry, or tuna jacket potato.
Dinner: fish, beans, lentils, eggs, poultry, meat, tofu, or another protein food alongside vegetables and carbohydrates.
Gentle takeaway: You do not need a complicated diet. Adding one protein source to ordinary meals is often a simple and realistic starting point.

lessons.title: Iron and folate: supporting blood and early development
body: Iron and folate are two of the most important nutrients discussed in pregnancy because they help with different but connected processes. Iron helps produce haemoglobin, the part of red blood cells that carries oxygen around the body. Folate, also called vitamin B9, helps cells divide and supports early development of the neural tube, the structure that becomes the brain and spinal cord.

During pregnancy, blood volume increases substantially. That means the body needs more iron to support the additional blood supply and the baby’s development. The reviewed nutrient guidance lists an iron requirement of 27 mg per day and a folate requirement of 600 micrograms per day during pregnancy. Iron deficiency becomes increasingly common later in pregnancy, with the review estimating that 10% to 20% of women may experience it by the third trimester.

Folate has special importance before conception and in the early weeks of pregnancy because the neural tube develops very early — sometimes before someone knows they are pregnant. This is why NHS-linked guidance commonly promotes folic-acid supplementation before pregnancy and through the first 12 weeks, alongside eating foods naturally rich in folate such as leafy green vegetables, eggs, walnuts, pulses, and fortified foods.

Iron-rich foods include meat, pulses, lentils, beans, dark green leafy vegetables, fortified breakfast cereals, and some dried fruit. The body absorbs iron from animal sources differently from plant sources, but combining plant-based iron foods with vitamin C foods — for example, peppers, tomatoes, berries, oranges, or kiwi — can support absorption. Tea and coffee with meals may reduce absorption because of compounds called tannins, so this is something users can discuss with a midwife or dietitian if iron levels are low.

Natal IQ should be careful not to turn symptoms into a self-diagnosis checklist. Tiredness is common in pregnancy for many reasons, but ongoing extreme fatigue, breathlessness, dizziness, paleness, or a racing heart can be mentioned at routine care appointments. A blood test, rather than an app, is what can assess iron status.
keyPoints: Iron helps carry oxygen through the expanded blood supply of pregnancy.
Folate supports early cell development and neural-tube development.
Iron deficiency and anaemia are common, especially later in pregnancy, and are routinely assessed by maternity teams.
A varied diet can include folate and iron, while supplements should be discussed in line with local healthcare guidance.
Feeling unusually exhausted is worth mentioning — not because it automatically means anaemia, but because professionals can check.
Gentle takeaway: Iron and folate are not about getting every meal “right.” They are steady, everyday nutrients that support your body while it is doing a remarkable amount of work.

lessons.title: Calcium and vitamin D: bone-building support
body: Calcium is often described as “for bones,” but in pregnancy it has a bigger story. The baby needs calcium to build a skeleton, and the mother’s body adapts to help make that calcium available. The nutrient review notes that the fetal skeleton accumulates around 30 g of calcium, largely during the third trimester when bone growth and mineralisation become more rapid.

Vitamin D helps the body absorb and use calcium. It therefore works alongside calcium in supporting healthy bone development. The reviewed recommendations list 1,000 mg calcium and 15 micrograms of vitamin D daily during pregnancy. In the UK, NHS-linked guidance commonly advises a daily vitamin D supplement during pregnancy, especially in seasons with less sunlight exposure; local guidance can vary, so the app should direct users to discuss their own needs with a pharmacist, midwife, or GP.

Calcium-rich foods do not have to be limited to dairy. Milk, yoghurt, and cheese are well-known options, but fortified plant drinks, tofu set with calcium, some fortified cereals, kale, broccoli, sesame seeds, almonds, and tinned fish with edible bones can contribute too. This matters because users may be lactose intolerant, vegan, culturally avoid certain foods, or simply dislike dairy.

Vitamin D is more difficult to get from food alone. Oily fish, egg yolks, fortified spreads, fortified breakfast cereals, and some fortified plant milks may provide it, while sunlight also contributes to vitamin D production. However, skin tone, season, time outdoors, sunscreen use, and where someone lives can all change how much vitamin D the body makes. This complexity is why personal healthcare advice is more appropriate than one-size-fits-all rules.

The tone here should remain calm. One day without yoghurt, a week of rain, or a changed appetite does not mean something has gone wrong. The goal is to explain why calcium and vitamin D matter and point users toward routine pregnancy guidance.
keyPoints: The baby’s bones grow and become more mineralised throughout pregnancy, especially later on.
Calcium and vitamin D work together in bone health.
Dairy foods are one source of calcium, but there are many alternatives.
Vitamin D advice can depend on local health guidance, diet, skin tone, season, and other factors.
Questions about supplements belong in conversations with a maternity team, GP, pharmacist, or dietitian.
Gentle takeaway: Think of calcium and vitamin D as quiet everyday support for a long-term job: helping your body and your baby build strong foundations.

lessons.title: Iodine, zinc, magnesium and vitamin B12
body: Nutrition is often reduced to a few headline nutrients, but pregnancy depends on many smaller nutrients working together. Iodine, zinc, magnesium, and vitamin B12 all play different roles in the background. They are less likely to be discussed in casual pregnancy conversations, yet they help explain why dietary variety matters.

Iodine is important for thyroid function and for fetal brain development. The nutrient review notes that iodine requirements rise by around 50% in pregnancy, reflecting the greater demands on the mother’s thyroid system and the baby’s developing brain. Sources may include dairy products, eggs, fish, seafood, and iodised salt where it is used. However, pregnancy nutrition advice should avoid encouraging users to take iodine supplements without checking local guidelines, especially if they have a thyroid condition.

Zinc helps with cell growth, immune function, and tissue repair. It is found in foods such as meat, poultry, beans, nuts, seeds, dairy, and whole grains. Magnesium contributes to many body functions, including muscle and nerve activity. Foods including nuts, seeds, legumes, wholegrains, leafy greens, and some fortified cereals can provide magnesium. The nutritional review notes research links between low magnesium status and conditions including hypertension, gestational diabetes, and preterm labour, but associations do not prove that a nutrient alone causes or prevents these outcomes.

Vitamin B12 supports the nervous system and red blood cells. It is naturally found mainly in animal-derived foods, such as meat, fish, eggs, dairy, and foods fortified with B12. This is particularly relevant for people who follow vegan diets or eat few animal products; it is not a reason to alarm users, but a good reason for the app to recommend discussion with a midwife, GP, or dietitian.

Natal IQ should make a clear distinction between “food education” and “supplement prescribing.” The app can teach where nutrients come from and why they matter. It should not tell someone to start, stop, or increase a supplement, because that choice can depend on health history, medication, test results, and local medical advice.
keyPoints: Iodine supports thyroid function and fetal brain development.
Zinc and magnesium contribute to growth, immune function, muscle activity, and many other processes.
Vitamin B12 is especially important to consider in plant-based diets.
Different food groups contribute different nutrients, so variety is usually more helpful than focusing on one “superfood.”
Supplements may be useful for some people, but individual advice should come from qualified healthcare professionals.
Gentle takeaway: Nutrition is less about finding one perfect food and more about building a varied pattern that gives your body many different building blocks.
sources: Jouanne M, et al. “Nutrient Requirements during Pregnancy and Lactation.” Used for iodine, zinc, magnesium, B12, and other pregnancy nutrient requirements.

lessons.title: Omega-3 and DHA: the brain-development story
body: Omega-3 fats are a family of fats that include DHA, short for docosahexaenoic acid. DHA is especially important because it becomes part of the developing brain and eyes. The pregnancy nutrient review explains that DHA accumulates in the fetal brain particularly from around the sixth month of pregnancy onward, when the brain is growing rapidly.

This is why fish often appears in pregnancy nutrition guidance. Oily fish, such as salmon, sardines, trout, and mackerel, can provide omega-3 fats as well as protein, vitamin D, and iodine. But pregnancy advice around fish can become confusing because some fish may contain higher levels of mercury. The useful message is not “fish is scary” or “all fish should be avoided.” It is that types and amounts matter, and users should follow local NHS-style guidance on fish choices and limits.

For those who do not eat fish, other foods can contribute omega-3 fats. Walnuts, chia seeds, flaxseed, rapeseed oil, and some fortified products contain plant-based omega-3. Algae-based products may also be relevant to some people, because algae is the original source of DHA in the marine food chain. Whether a supplement is appropriate is an individual conversation, particularly for people with allergies, dietary restrictions, or existing health conditions.

The science should be phrased responsibly. Research has linked low DHA intake with later cognitive and behavioural outcomes, but no single food determines a child’s intelligence, personality, health, or future. Natal IQ must avoid language that makes a pregnant person feel they are “building a smarter baby” with food. That message is inaccurate and emotionally harmful.

Instead, the app can use the gentler language: “Omega-3 fats are one part of a varied diet that supports normal brain and eye development.” It makes the content useful without turning food into a performance test.
keyPoints: DHA is an omega-3 fat that supports fetal brain and eye development.
The baby accumulates DHA especially during later pregnancy.
Low-mercury fish choices can be part of a healthy pregnancy diet, following local guidance.
Plant-based food sources and algae-derived options may be relevant for those who do not eat fish.
No nutrient or single food can predict a baby’s intelligence or guarantee an outcome.
Gentle takeaway: Food supports development, but pregnancy is not a test you pass by eating perfectly. Consistent, realistic choices matter far more than perfection.
sources: Jouanne M, et al. “Nutrient Requirements during Pregnancy and Lactation.” Used for DHA and fetal brain accumulation.

NHS Inform. “Eating well in pregnancy.” Used for practical pregnancy dietary guidance.

lessons.title: Carbohydrates, fibre and steady energy
body: Carbohydrates are often made to sound like a problem, but they are a major source of energy for the body. During pregnancy, when your body is working continuously, carbohydrates can help provide fuel for you and your developing baby. The more useful conversation is not whether carbohydrates are “good” or “bad,” but which types of carbohydrate you eat and what you pair them with.

Fibre-rich carbohydrates include oats, brown rice, wholemeal bread, wholewheat pasta, potatoes with skin, beans, lentils, vegetables, fruit, and some breakfast cereals. Fibre supports digestion and may help with constipation, which is a very common pregnancy symptom. It also tends to make meals more filling and can reduce the sharp rise-and-fall feeling some people get after sugary foods.

Refined carbohydrates, such as sweets, biscuits, sugary drinks, white bread, or pastries, are not morally “bad.” They are simply often less filling and may not offer as many vitamins, minerals, or fibre. A balanced approach can help users move away from guilt: it is okay to enjoy food, and it is also useful to understand which foods provide long-lasting energy.

Pairing carbohydrates with a protein or healthy fat source can make a snack or meal feel more satisfying. Examples include fruit with yoghurt, toast with egg, crackers with hummus, porridge with nuts, or rice with beans. This is an educational pattern, not a treatment plan for gestational diabetes or another condition. Anyone with a diagnosed condition should receive personalised advice from their care team.

Pregnancy cravings can complicate this topic. Craving bread, sweets, salty snacks, or particular foods does not prove a nutrient deficiency, reveal the baby’s sex, or mean someone is doing pregnancy wrong. Cravings are common and may be influenced by hormones, nausea, culture, routine, comfort, and appetite changes.
keyPoints: Carbohydrates provide energy and do not need to be eliminated in pregnancy.
Wholegrain and fibre-rich options can support digestion and longer-lasting fullness.
Pairing carbohydrate foods with protein and fat can make meals feel more balanced.
Constipation is common in pregnancy, and fibre and fluids are often part of the wider conversation.
A person with gestational diabetes or another condition needs individual advice rather than a generic app plan.
Gentle takeaway: Carbs are fuel. A calmer goal is choosing more fibre-rich options most of the time — not cutting out foods you enjoy.
sources: NHS Inform. “Eating well in pregnancy.” Used for balanced eating, food groups, and general pregnancy nutrition.
NHS. “Gestational diabetes.” Used for the need for professional assessment and personalised management rather than a generic app plan.
Jouanne M, et al. “Nutrient Requirements during Pregnancy and Lactation.” Used for broader pregnancy-nutrition context.

lessons.title: A flexible day of pregnancy nutrition
body: Nutrition advice becomes useful when it feels possible on a tired Tuesday, during nausea, with a tight food budget, or when someone simply has no energy to cook. This lesson is not a meal prescription. It is an example of how ordinary foods can combine to cover several nutritional needs over one day.

Breakfast could be porridge made with milk or a fortified alternative, topped with banana and nuts. This offers carbohydrates for energy, calcium from milk or a fortified substitute, and fats and protein from nuts. Another breakfast could be eggs on wholegrain toast with tomatoes or fruit, combining protein, iron, carbohydrates, and vitamin C.

Lunch could be a lentil soup with bread, a chicken or tofu wrap with salad, a baked potato with beans and cheese, or a rice bowl with vegetables and chickpeas. The aim is not a perfect recipe. It is to show that meals can include a protein food, a carbohydrate food, and some fruit or vegetables without becoming expensive or complicated.

A snack can be as simple as yoghurt and fruit, hummus and crackers, cheese and oatcakes, peanut butter on toast, a boiled egg, or a handful of nuts. Snacks are especially relevant because nausea, heartburn, and a growing uterus may make large meals uncomfortable. Smaller, regular eating can feel more manageable for many people.

Dinner might include salmon with potatoes and vegetables, a bean chilli with rice, a pasta sauce with lentils, a chicken traybake, or a tofu stir-fry. These examples include different cultural and dietary patterns on purpose. A useful app should not assume everyone eats the same foods, has the same budget, or enjoys cooking.

Natal IQ could make this interactive without becoming prescriptive: users could tap dietary preferences, common aversions, allergies, or foods they dislike, and the app could show alternative meal ideas while displaying a note that information is general and should not replace individual dietary advice.
keyPoints: A balanced day can be built from ordinary, accessible foods.
Meals do not need to be complicated to contain protein, fibre, fruit or vegetables, and key nutrients.
Snacks can play an important role when appetite is low or large meals feel uncomfortable.
Cultural foods, vegetarian meals, convenience foods, and simple meals can all fit into a healthy pattern.
A varied week matters more than trying to create a nutritionally perfect day.
Gentle takeaway: Think “good enough and varied,” not “Instagram-perfect.” Food should support your day, not become another source of pressure.

lessons.title: Hydration and pregnancy comfort
body: Water is part of almost every system in the body, and it becomes particularly relevant in pregnancy because blood volume increases significantly. Hydration supports circulation, digestion, temperature regulation, and kidney function. It may also help some people feel more comfortable when dealing with constipation, headaches, tiredness, or dry mouth.

There is no single number that fits every person. Fluid needs may change depending on weather, activity, sickness, whether someone is breastfeeding after birth, and how much fluid they get from food. Instead of demanding a fixed amount, Natal IQ can encourage users to notice practical signs: are they regularly drinking through the day, do they feel thirsty, and are they able to keep fluids down?

Water is the straightforward baseline. Milk and fortified plant drinks can contribute fluid as well as nutrients such as calcium. Soups, fruit, yoghurt, and watery vegetables also add fluid to a person’s daily intake. Tea and coffee count toward fluid intake too, but caffeine limits still matter; NHS guidance says pregnant people should have no more than 200 mg caffeine a day.

Sugary drinks can be refreshing, especially when nausea makes water difficult, but they may provide a lot of sugar without keeping someone full. Energy drinks can contain high caffeine and other ingredients that are less suitable in pregnancy. The app should not shame someone for having a drink they enjoy; it can simply explain why water, milk, and lower-sugar options are usually more helpful as everyday choices.

A very important safety boundary: the app should never tell a user that hydration will solve severe symptoms. If someone cannot keep fluids down, has severe vomiting, feels faint, or is worried about dehydration, Natal IQ should direct them to contact their maternity team or urgent care.
keyPoints: Pregnancy increases the importance of regular fluid intake because blood volume and body demands change.
Water is a practical default, but many foods and drinks contribute to hydration.
Caffeine includes coffee, tea, cola, energy drinks, chocolate, and some medicines, not only coffee.
NHS guidance advises no more than 200 mg of caffeine per day in pregnancy.
Severe vomiting, inability to keep fluids down, or feeling very unwell needs professional advice rather than self-management through an app.
Gentle takeaway: Keep a drink nearby, sip regularly, and let hydration be a small act of care rather than another number to achieve.

NHS Inform. “Eating well in pregnancy.” Used for general healthy-eating and drink guidance.

lessons.title: Food safety without food fear
body: Pregnancy food guidance can easily become overwhelming. People may hear long lists of “don’ts,” worry about something they already ate, and begin feeling that everyday food is dangerous. Natal IQ should take the opposite approach: explain the few major areas of concern clearly, calmly, and without judgement.

The main reasons some foods need care during pregnancy are infection risk and contaminants such as mercury. Foods that are raw or undercooked may carry bacteria or parasites. Unpasteurised milk products can carry harmful bacteria. Some fish have higher mercury levels, which is why guidance distinguishes between types of fish rather than banning fish entirely. NHS food-safety guidance covers categories including dairy, meat, poultry, eggs, fish and seafood, fruit and vegetables, caffeine, and drinks.

This is also an opportunity to teach basic food hygiene: wash fruit and vegetables, keep raw meat separate from ready-to-eat food, cook meat thoroughly, check use-by dates, and store chilled foods safely. These practices are useful for everyone, not only pregnant people, and can make the topic feel empowering rather than restrictive.

The app should avoid presenting food safety as a “good mother/bad mother” scorecard. Eating a food before realising it was on a caution list does not automatically mean harm has occurred. If a user is worried about a specific food exposure, they should contact a midwife, GP, pharmacist, NHS 111, or another appropriate local health service for individual advice.

A good design pattern would be a “food guidance explained” page. Users select a broad category — cheese, eggs, fish, meat, drinks, or food hygiene — then receive NHS-aligned information, the reason for the guidance, and a “Need personalised advice?” button leading to suitable professional contacts.
keyPoints: Food-safety guidance mainly exists because of infection risk and contaminants, not because ordinary food is dangerous.
The important categories include unpasteurised dairy, raw or undercooked animal products, high-mercury fish, and alcohol.
Hygiene practices such as handwashing, proper cooking, and safe storage matter.
Fish is not an all-or-nothing issue; the type and amount are relevant.
If someone is worried about something they ate, the right next step is a professional conversation, not panic or self-diagnosis.
Gentle takeaway: Food safety should give you clarity, not fear. Learn the few key cautions, then return to enjoying normal meals.
sources: NHS. “Foods to avoid in pregnancy.” Primary source for UK food-safety, fish, dairy, caffeine, alcohol, and food-handling information.

lessons.title: Nausea, aversions and the “survival weeks”
body: Nausea is one of the best-known pregnancy symptoms, but knowing it is common does not make it easy. It can change what food smells like, what textures feel tolerable, how much someone can eat at once, and even how they feel about foods they usually love. Food aversions can be frustrating, especially when someone is trying hard to “eat well.”

For many people, nausea is strongest in the first trimester, though it can occur at any time of day and may last longer for some. Ordinary nausea may improve with small, frequent meals, avoiding foods that trigger a strong reaction, choosing bland or cold foods, and not letting the stomach become completely empty. These are common comfort strategies, not medical treatment instructions.

When a person is in a nausea-heavy period, the most useful nutritional approach may be “what can I tolerate today?” Dry toast, crackers, rice, potatoes, fruit, yoghurt, soup, cereal, or plain pasta can be more realistic than a carefully planned meal. Natal IQ should reassure users that a short period of less-than-ideal eating does not mean they have damaged their pregnancy.

However, the app must clearly distinguish everyday nausea from symptoms needing professional support. Hyperemesis gravidarum is a more severe form of nausea and vomiting that can make it difficult to keep food or fluids down and can lead to dehydration. Someone who cannot keep fluids down, is vomiting persistently, feels faint, notices very dark urine, or is concerned should contact their maternity team, GP, or urgent-care service.

This module could include an “I need help now” button that does not diagnose but makes appropriate contacts easy to find. This aligns perfectly with Natal IQ’s purpose: reducing the barrier to reaching out.
keyPoints: Nausea and aversions are common and can make ordinary healthy eating temporarily difficult.
Small, frequent foods may be easier than large meals for some people.
“Fed is better than perfect” is a reasonable mindset during difficult nausea weeks.
Severe or persistent vomiting is not something someone should manage alone.
Professional support is available for symptoms that affect hydration, weight, or daily functioning.
Gentle takeaway: Your body is not failing because it only tolerates plain food today. Be kind to yourself, and reach out if nausea becomes hard to manage.
sources: NICE. “Antenatal care: recommendations.” Used for information on nausea and vomiting in pregnancy, including mild-to-moderate symptoms and escalation for severe vomiting/hyperemesis.

lessons.title: Weight gain: trends, not judgement
body: Pregnancy weight can be one of the most emotionally loaded topics in maternity care. Some people fear gaining too much; others worry they are not gaining enough; many feel uncomfortable being weighed or discussing their body. Natal IQ should present the topic as health education, never as a target, score, or judgement.

Weight gain during pregnancy includes much more than the baby. It can include the placenta, amniotic fluid, increased blood volume, breast tissue, the uterus, fluid stores, and body-fat stores that support pregnancy and breastfeeding. The nutrient review describes a typical gestational gain of around 11–16 kg for women who begin pregnancy in a normal BMI range, while the appropriate range differs depending on pre-pregnancy body size and individual circumstances.

A number on the scale also naturally moves up and down due to fluid changes, time of day, food, constipation, swelling, and clothing. That is why maternity teams look at the overall pattern alongside many other pieces of information, such as blood pressure, symptoms, scans, fetal growth, and medical history. One weigh-in cannot describe the health of a pregnancy.

Natal IQ should not include automatic “ideal weight gain” calculations unless these are designed and clinically approved with obstetric expertise. A generic target may create anxiety, worsen body-image concerns, or fail to account for twins, eating disorders, diabetes, pre-existing conditions, ethnicity, adolescent pregnancy, or other relevant factors.

A better feature would be a private “questions for my appointment” tool: “I’m worried about appetite,” “I have not gained weight recently,” “I’m worried I’m gaining quickly,” or “I find weigh-ins stressful.” The app can help users prepare to discuss concerns without interpreting their measurements.
keyPoints: Pregnancy-related weight reflects many normal body changes, not just the baby or food intake.
A typical range exists, but appropriate gain differs between individuals.
Healthcare teams assess overall patterns and context, not one isolated number.
Weight concerns can connect to nausea, food access, body image, mental health, and existing conditions.
An app should encourage a conversation with a care team rather than giving individual targets.
Gentle takeaway: Your pregnancy is not a scale score. Your care team looks at the full picture, and you deserve support if weight conversations feel difficult.
sources: Jouanne M, et al. “Nutrient Requirements during Pregnancy and Lactation.” Used for gestational weight gain and pregnancy physiology.
PMC. “Acceptability of the FIGO Nutrition Checklist in Preconception and Early Pregnancy.” Used for nutrition and weight-conversation context.
NICE. “Antenatal care: recommendations.” Used for booking assessment, height/weight measurement, and individualised care.

lessons.title: Food information when a condition is present
body: Pregnancy can come with conditions such as gestational diabetes, anaemia, high blood pressure, thyroid disease, coeliac disease, hyperemesis, or food allergies. When a condition is present, nutrition may become part of the care plan. But that does not mean one generic diet works for everyone.

For example, someone with gestational diabetes may receive guidance on meal timing, carbohydrate portions, food combinations, glucose monitoring, movement, and medication if needed. Someone with anaemia may discuss iron-rich foods, iron supplements, and follow-up blood tests. A person with coeliac disease may need to maintain a gluten-free diet, while someone with severe nausea may focus first on hydration and foods they can tolerate.

The key message is that these are personalised conversations. Health conditions, blood-test results, medications, cultural dietary patterns, allergies, cost, access to food, and pregnancy stage can all affect what advice is appropriate. Natal IQ can explain the vocabulary and help users prepare questions, but it should never give a meal plan that acts as treatment.
A useful app feature would be “Questions to take to your appointment.” For instance:
• “What does this result mean in my situation?”
• “Do I need a dietitian referral?”
• “Are there foods or supplements I should ask about?”
• “How will we monitor this?”
• “Who should I contact if I have questions between appointments?”
This makes the app useful without creating legal or clinical risk. It respects medical expertise while making healthcare conversations easier to enter.
keyPoints: Conditions can change which nutritional topics receive more attention.
Gestational diabetes, anaemia, thyroid conditions, allergies, and severe nausea all need individualised advice.
The purpose of food changes in care plans is support, not blame.
Medical test results must be interpreted by qualified professionals.
Preparing thoughtful questions can make appointments feel less overwhelming.
Gentle takeaway: If your pregnancy includes a condition, you do not need to become your own clinician. Natal IQ can help you understand the conversation; your care team will guide the plan.
sources: NHS. “Gestational diabetes.” Used for GDM screening, diagnosis, and care.
Jouanne M, et al. “Nutrient Requirements during Pregnancy and Lactation.” Used for broader nutrient context.
PMC review. “Safety and efficacy of supplements in pregnancy.” Used for careful supplement language.
NICE. “Antenatal care: recommendations.” Used for individual risk assessment, screening, and personalised care.

lessons.title: Nutrition after birth and recovery
body: Nutrition does not stop mattering after birth. The postnatal period can involve physical recovery, sleep disruption, emotional change, feeding a baby, and often a sudden drop in time and energy for cooking. The aim of postnatal food support is not “getting your body back.” It is helping a recovering person have enough energy, hydration, and nourishment.

The Cleveland Clinic’s postpartum overview describes the postnatal period as beginning immediately after childbirth and extending through a recovery period that can involve bleeding, wound healing, breast changes, constipation, fatigue, and emotional adjustment. Food cannot solve all of these, but regular meals and fluids can support everyday functioning while the body heals.

Protein-containing foods can support tissue repair. Fibre-rich foods and enough fluid may help with constipation. Iron may remain relevant after blood loss, depending on someone’s individual health and lab results. If someone chooses to breastfeed, food and hydration are still important, but they do not need a perfect “breastfeeding diet.” Their needs should be discussed with their health visitor, midwife, GP, or dietitian if there are concerns.

This is also where practical support becomes a health issue. The Orlando Health resource emphasises fatigue and suggests arranging support, including meal preparation and help from trusted people, during the early weeks after birth. Natal IQ can turn that into a practical feature: a shared support list where a partner, family member, or friend can sign up to bring food, do shopping, or help with chores.

For pregnancies affected by a suspected or confirmed Down syndrome diagnosis, support planning may be especially important. The St George’s NHS pathway highlights emotional support, neonatal planning, breastfeeding support, and collaborative care for families. Natal IQ should offer contacts and support routes, not imply that food can alter the diagnosis or outcome.
keyPoints: The postnatal period is a recovery period for the mother, not only a care period for the baby.
Easy food, hydration, fibre, and protein can make daily recovery more manageable.
Breastfeeding does not require perfection or a special “magic” diet.
Practical help with meals and chores is a legitimate form of postpartum support.
Ongoing symptoms, low mood, feeding worries, or recovery concerns should be discussed with the postnatal care team.
Gentle takeaway: After birth, simple food and practical support count. Recovery deserves the same care and attention as pregnancy.
sources: Cleveland Clinic. “Postpartum: Stages, Symptoms & Recovery Time.” Used for postpartum stages, symptoms, and recovery.
NHS. “Your body after the birth.” Used for postnatal bleeding, stitches, bladder and bowel changes, and urgent symptoms.
Orlando Health. “New Mom? Watch for These 10 Things That Can Happen After Giving Birth.” Used for postnatal symptoms and practical support planning.
St George’s NHS / DSRF-UK. “Personalised antenatal care of pregnancies suspected or diagnosed with Down syndrome.” Used for neonatal, feeding, breastfeeding, and family-support considerations.

lessons.title: Preeclampsia: why blood-pressure checks matter
body: Preeclampsia is a pregnancy condition involving high blood pressure and changes that can affect organs, including the kidneys. It is one reason antenatal appointments commonly include a blood-pressure reading and a urine sample. These routine checks are designed to notice patterns early, not to create worry.

The word “preeclampsia” can sound frightening, but the first thing Natal IQ should explain is why routine care is protective. A maternity team looks at the whole picture: blood pressure over time, urine findings, symptoms, medical history, blood tests, fetal growth, and pregnancy stage. A single reading, a swollen ankle, or a moment of feeling tired cannot diagnose preeclampsia.

Some symptoms are important to know because they are reasons to contact a maternity team promptly. These can include severe headache, visual changes such as flashing lights or blurred vision, pain below the ribs, sudden swelling of the face or hands, feeling very unwell, or concerns about fetal movement. These symptoms can have several causes. In pregnancy, it is important to contact the maternity team for advice rather than trying to work out the cause alone.

Preeclampsia risk can be influenced by many factors, including a first pregnancy, previous preeclampsia, multiple pregnancy, chronic high blood pressure, kidney disease, diabetes, and autoimmune conditions. But risk factors are not predictions. Many people with risk factors do not develop it, and people without obvious risk factors can still be monitored routinely.

Natal IQ should never ask a user to “score” themselves for preeclampsia or show a result saying that they are low risk or high risk. The correct role of the app is to explain why routine checks happen and make it easier for users to contact a professional when symptoms concern them.
keyPoints: Preeclampsia involves high blood pressure and can affect pregnancy health.
Routine blood-pressure and urine checks are a protective part of antenatal care.
A single number or one symptom does not establish a diagnosis.
Certain severe symptoms should prompt a call to a maternity team, NHS 111, or urgent care as appropriate.
Management, testing, and treatment must be led by qualified maternity professionals.
Gentle takeaway: Routine blood-pressure checks are not a test you pass or fail. They are one of the ways your care team looks after you.
sources: NICE. “Antenatal care: recommendations.” States that blood pressure should be measured at every routine face-to-face antenatal appointment and that urine dipstick testing should be offered for proteinuria.
NHS. “Your antenatal care and appointments.” Covers routine blood-pressure and urine checks in antenatal care.
NHS 111 Wales. “Routine checks and tests.” Explains blood-pressure and urine checks and their relevance to preeclampsia.
National Academies / NCBI Bookshelf. “Risks to Maternal Health.” Provides broader maternal-health context, including hypertension and preeclampsia.

lessons.title: Gestational diabetes: understanding the screening conversation
body: Gestational diabetes, often shortened to GDM, means that blood glucose levels are higher than expected during pregnancy. Pregnancy hormones can affect how the body responds to insulin, the hormone that helps move glucose from the bloodstream into cells for energy. This is not simply caused by eating sugar, and a diagnosis is not a sign that someone has “done pregnancy wrong.”

Some people are offered screening because of their medical history, previous pregnancy history, family history, body-size considerations, certain scan findings, ethnicity, or other factors used in local maternity guidance. Being offered a test often reflects routine risk assessment rather than a prediction that something is wrong.

The glucose tolerance test is usually discussed during the second trimester. The exact process varies by maternity trust, but it commonly involves fasting, an initial blood sample, drinking a measured glucose solution, waiting, and having further blood testing. The purpose is to see how the body processes glucose over time. It can be time-consuming and not especially enjoyable, but knowing the steps beforehand can make it less intimidating.

If GDM is diagnosed, maternity teams may discuss food patterns, blood-glucose monitoring, activity, appointments, fetal monitoring, and sometimes medication. The details differ from person to person. Natal IQ can explain the vocabulary, offer appointment-question prompts, and create reminder tools, but it should not provide a treatment meal plan or interpret glucose readings.
It is important to keep the language non-blaming. Pregnancy hormones can affect insulin resistance, and a diagnosis is not evidence that someone ate badly, lacked discipline, or caused the condition.
keyPoints: GDM is about how the body handles glucose during pregnancy hormones.
It is often discovered through screening rather than symptoms.
A test invitation is not blame and does not mean a person caused the condition.
Care may involve several forms of support, depending on individual circumstances.
Medical interpretation of results and management plans belongs with the maternity care team.
sources: NHS. “Gestational diabetes.” Primary source for risk factors, oral glucose tolerance testing, diagnosis, treatment, and follow-up.
NICE. “Antenatal care: recommendations.” States that people assessed as at risk of GDM should be offered an oral glucose tolerance test between 24 and 28 weeks.
NHS. “Your antenatal care and appointments.” Covers GDM screening within antenatal care.
NHS 111 Wales. “Routine checks and tests.” Provides supporting information on GDM testing.

extras.heading: Useful appointment questions
items: “Why was this screening recommended for me?”
“If my result is outside the expected range, what happens next?”
“Can I speak with a diabetes midwife or dietitian?”
“Who should I contact if I am worried between appointments?”
Gentle takeaway: A GDM test is a way of learning more about how your body is responding to pregnancy — not a judgement about what you ate.

lessons.title: Anaemia and iron deficiency
body: Anaemia occurs when the blood does not have enough healthy red blood cells or haemoglobin to carry oxygen effectively. In pregnancy, iron deficiency is a common cause because the body’s blood volume expands and iron needs increase. The pregnancy nutrient review estimates that iron deficiency may affect around 10% to 20% of women by the third trimester.

Fatigue is one of the most common symptoms of pregnancy, so it can be difficult to know whether tiredness is “normal” or something worth checking. Anaemia can also be associated with paleness, shortness of breath, dizziness, headaches, palpitations, or low energy. However, none of these symptoms can confirm anaemia on their own. Blood tests are what allow maternity teams to assess iron levels and look at other possible causes.

This lesson should explain why blood tests may be offered at booking, later in pregnancy, or when a care professional thinks they are needed. The purpose is not to catch someone out. It is to identify whether the body needs additional support. If anaemia is found, the care team may discuss food sources of iron, supplements, possible causes of the deficiency, and follow-up testing.

Natal IQ can connect this lesson to the Iron and Folate nutrition lesson. It can explain that pulses, beans, lentils, meat, fortified cereals, and leafy greens can contribute iron, while vitamin C can help support absorption of iron from plant foods. However, the app must not say that food alone will treat a diagnosed deficiency or tell users how much supplementation to take.

This lesson is also a chance to validate tiredness. Pregnancy fatigue is often dismissed. A user should feel allowed to say, “I am more exhausted than I expected,” even if the eventual explanation is simply that pregnancy is demanding.
keyPoints: Iron deficiency is a common reason for anaemia in pregnancy.
Increased blood volume creates greater demand for iron.
Symptoms can overlap with normal pregnancy tiredness, so blood tests matter.
A diagnosed deficiency can be assessed and managed with professional support.
Mentioning severe or persistent fatigue is appropriate and useful.
Gentle takeaway: Tiredness is common, but you never need to minimise how you feel. Bringing it up gives your care team a chance to check what is going on.
sources: Jouanne M, et al. “Nutrient Requirements during Pregnancy and Lactation.” Used for iron requirements and the discussion of iron deficiency in pregnancy.
NICE. “Antenatal care: recommendations.” Recommends full blood count testing at the first antenatal appointment and again at 28 weeks.
Leeds Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust. “Food and activity support for a healthy pregnancy.” Provides NHS-linked nutrition and folic-acid information.
Health Service Executive. “Healthy eating during pregnancy.” Provides practical food and iron-absorption information.

lessons.title: Hyperemesis gravidarum and severe nausea
body: Nausea and vomiting are often casually called “morning sickness,” even though symptoms can occur at any time of day. For many people, symptoms are unpleasant but manageable. For others, nausea and vomiting become severe enough to interfere with eating, drinking, work, rest, and everyday functioning. This more severe pattern is known as hyperemesis gravidarum.

It is important for Natal IQ to validate both experiences. Mild nausea can still feel miserable, and severe nausea is not a sign of being dramatic, weak, or unable to cope. It is a physical condition that deserves support. People with hyperemesis may struggle to keep fluids down, vomit frequently, lose weight, become dehydrated, and feel isolated or distressed.

The app should avoid giving a rigid threshold such as “vomit X times.” Instead, it should focus on the effect on the person: “Are you unable to keep fluids down?” “Are you feeling faint?” “Is nausea stopping you from functioning?” “Are you worried?” These are appropriate reasons to contact a maternity team.

Care may include hydration assessment, urine or blood testing, anti-sickness medication, dietary advice, and, for some people, hospital treatment. This is why the app should be a bridge to care, not a substitute for it. A “contact your maternity team” prompt should be visible throughout this lesson.

Severe nausea can also make pregnancy feel lonely or joyless, particularly when other people expect the pregnant person to feel excited. The Calm & Connect section should link here with a reminder that support can include practical help, not just reassurance: food drop-offs, help with housework, childcare, or someone accompanying the person to an appointment.
keyPoints: Nausea is common, but severe and persistent vomiting needs attention.
Hyperemesis can affect hydration, nutrition, mood, work, and daily life.
Difficulty keeping fluids down, feeling faint, or being worried are good reasons to seek professional advice.
Treatment and support exist; someone does not need to simply endure it.
Practical and emotional support are both meaningful during a difficult symptom period.
Gentle takeaway: Severe nausea is not something to “prove” or push through. If it is taking over your day, your maternity team deserves to know.
sources: NICE. “Antenatal care: recommendations.” Covers mild-to-moderate nausea, antiemetic discussions, fluids, and inpatient care for severe vomiting/hyperemesis.
RCOG. “The Management of Nausea and Vomiting of Pregnancy and Hyperemesis Gravidarum.” Specialist clinical guidance on nausea and hyperemesis.
NICE. “Antenatal care: recommendations.” Supports personalised, compassionate, and non-judgemental antenatal information.

lessons.title: UTIs, vaginal symptoms and feeling comfortable asking
body: Pregnancy changes the urinary tract and vaginal environment in ways that can make infections or irritation more likely. These can be awkward topics to raise, but they are ordinary health concerns and maternity professionals discuss them every day.

A urinary tract infection, often called a UTI, can cause pain or burning when urinating, a need to urinate more often, cloudy or strong-smelling urine, lower tummy discomfort, or feeling unwell. Vaginal infections or irritation can sometimes involve unusual discharge, itching, soreness, changed smell, or pain. Symptoms can have several causes, so the purpose of the lesson is not to name the condition from a symptom description.

In pregnancy, it is useful to mention symptoms early because some infections need assessment and treatment. The app can encourage users to contact their GP, midwife, or maternity assessment service, depending on the local pathway. It should not recommend over-the-counter treatment, leftover medication, or home remedies as substitutes for clinical assessment.

The tone matters. Users may feel embarrassed, worry they have done something wrong, or fear being judged for sexual activity, hygiene, or discharge. Natal IQ can actively reduce shame: changes in discharge, bladder symptoms, itching, and discomfort are health topics — not personal failures.
A useful interaction could be a “How to say it” prompt:
• “I have pain when I wee.”
• “I have noticed a change in discharge.”
• “I have itching or soreness.”
• “I feel worried about a possible infection.”
This lowers the barrier to reaching out without asking the app to diagnose.
keyPoints: Bladder and vaginal symptoms are common topics in pregnancy care.
Symptoms can have many causes, and a health professional is needed to assess them.
Burning urine, unusual discharge, itching, soreness, pain, fever, or feeling unwell are worth mentioning.
Early contact is supportive and can prevent a concern from becoming more uncomfortable.
There is no need to feel embarrassed; professionals are there to help.
Gentle takeaway: If something feels different or uncomfortable, you do not need the perfect words. “I’m worried about a symptom” is enough to start the conversation.
sources: NICE. “Antenatal care: recommendations.” Covers symptomatic vaginal discharge in pregnancy, including symptoms that may suggest infection and require investigation.
NHS. “Your antenatal care and appointments.” Covers routine urine testing within antenatal care.
NHS 111 Wales. “Routine checks and tests.” Gives supporting information about urine samples at antenatal appointments.

lessons.title: High blood pressure in pregnancy
body: Blood pressure is the force of blood moving through blood vessels. Pregnancy naturally changes circulation: the body makes more blood, the heart pumps more, and blood vessels adapt. This is why blood-pressure measurement is a routine part of antenatal care.

Some people have high blood pressure before pregnancy, known as chronic hypertension. Others develop raised blood pressure during pregnancy. Healthcare teams use timing, repeated readings, symptoms, urine tests, blood tests, medical history, and fetal monitoring to understand what is happening. An app cannot do this safely, and no user should be encouraged to diagnose themselves from one home reading.

Home blood-pressure monitoring may be part of care for some people, but it should always follow instructions from their own clinical team. Natal IQ could offer a neutral log for people whose clinician has asked them to monitor, but it should not interpret values or colour-code them as “safe” or “unsafe” unless the feature is clinically governed, validated, and linked to a care pathway.

It can be helpful to explain that high blood pressure is often symptomless, which is one reason appointments matter. When symptoms such as severe headache, vision changes, pain below the ribs, sudden swelling, or feeling very unwell appear in pregnancy, they should be treated as reasons to contact a maternity team promptly because they need clinical assessment.

The message should remain reassuring: most antenatal blood-pressure checks are normal, and checks are not signs that something is necessarily suspected. They are a routine way of looking after maternal health.
keyPoints: Pregnancy changes circulation, making blood-pressure monitoring routine.
Chronic hypertension and pregnancy-related hypertension are different clinical situations.
A single reading cannot explain the full picture.
Home monitoring should only be used as agreed with a healthcare professional.
Significant symptoms or worries should be discussed with the maternity team promptly.
Gentle takeaway: Blood-pressure checks are one of the quiet ways maternity care keeps an eye on wellbeing. You are not expected to interpret the numbers alone.
sources: NICE. “Antenatal care: recommendations.” Recommends BP measurement at every routine face-to-face appointment and explains referral for hypertension.
NHS. “Your antenatal care and appointments.” Covers blood-pressure checks within routine antenatal care.
NHS 111 Wales. “Routine checks and tests.” Provides an NHS explanation of BP monitoring in pregnancy.
National Academies / NCBI Bookshelf. “Risks to Maternal Health.” Provides broader maternal-hypertension context.

lessons.title: Preterm labour, membranes and reduced movement
body: A full-term pregnancy is generally considered to reach 37 weeks, so “preterm” means labour or birth occurring before then. The possibility of early labour can feel frightening, which is why Natal IQ should present this lesson calmly, clearly, and with an emphasis on prompt professional contact rather than symptom searching.

Possible signs that are worth contacting a maternity team about can include regular tightenings or contractions, period-like cramps, unusual backache, a sudden gush or trickle of fluid, vaginal bleeding, or a noticeable reduction or change in a baby’s usual movements. These symptoms do not automatically mean preterm labour or a problem with the placenta. They can have different explanations. But in pregnancy, it is appropriate to ask.

The St George’s DS care pathway is particularly relevant to Natal IQ because it describes a higher risk of preterm birth in pregnancies with a suspected or confirmed Down syndrome diagnosis, estimating that around 20% deliver before 37 weeks. It also describes the role of detailed antenatal assessment and personalised monitoring, including attention to fetal anomalies, amniotic fluid, growth, and placental function.

For a broader pregnancy-app audience, this lesson should not imply that every person with a suspected DS diagnosis will experience preterm labour. It should explain why personalised care plans exist: health teams adapt monitoring based on each pregnancy’s findings and family needs.

Reduced fetal movement deserves especially clear wording. Natal IQ should never say “wait and see,” “have something sweet,” or “try a cold drink first.” The app should state: if you think your baby’s movements have reduced or changed from their usual pattern, contact your maternity unit immediately. NHS guidance says not to wait until the next day.
keyPoints: Preterm labour concerns should be assessed by maternity professionals rather than judged by an app.
Cramps, contractions, fluid loss, bleeding, persistent backache, and changed movement can be reasons to call.
A change in a baby’s usual movement pattern should be raised immediately with the maternity unit.
Pregnancies differ, so monitoring plans are personalised.
In suspected or confirmed DS pregnancies, additional specialist care may be offered because the risk profile can differ.
Gentle takeaway: You do not need to be certain that something is wrong before contacting your maternity team. A call for reassurance is part of pregnancy care.
sources: NHS. “Your baby’s movements.” States that there is no set number of movements and that users should call their midwife or maternity unit immediately for reduced, stopped, or changed movements.

RCOG. “Reduced Fetal Movements.” States that there is insufficient evidence to recommend formal movement counting with specified alarm limits and emphasises awareness of the individual baby’s pattern.
NICE. “Antenatal care: recommendations.” Advises maternity contact at any time if there are concerns about baby movements after 24 weeks.
St George’s NHS / DSRF-UK. “Personalised antenatal care of pregnancies suspected or diagnosed with Down syndrome.” Discusses increased prematurity risk and specialist monitoring.

lessons.title: Thyroid health and hormonal changes
body: The thyroid is a small gland in the neck that produces hormones involved in energy use, temperature regulation, metabolism, and growth. Pregnancy changes many hormone systems, including the thyroid system. For some people, an existing thyroid condition needs closer monitoring during pregnancy; for others, a thyroid issue may first be noticed through routine blood tests or symptoms.

An underactive thyroid is called hypothyroidism, while an overactive thyroid is called hyperthyroidism. Both can have symptoms that overlap with ordinary pregnancy experiences: tiredness, changes in energy, feeling hot or cold, palpitations, nausea, weight change, and anxiety. That overlap is exactly why symptom lists should not be used to self-diagnose.

Iodine is relevant because it is used to make thyroid hormones, and iodine needs increase in pregnancy. But this does not mean everyone should independently take extra iodine. People with thyroid disorders, dietary restrictions, or medications need personalised professional advice because supplements and medication management can be complex.

Natal IQ can help users understand appointment language. For example: “thyroid function test,” “TSH,” “T4,” “medication review,” or “endocrinology referral.” It can explain that more blood tests or medication changes do not necessarily mean something is wrong; they may reflect the fact that pregnancy changes the body’s hormone needs.

This module can also link to emotional wellbeing. Thyroid symptoms and anxiety can overlap, and both deserve respectful attention. If a user feels persistently unwell, has a known thyroid condition, or is worried about medication, the app should invite them to contact the appropriate clinician.
keyPoints: The thyroid helps regulate metabolism and is relevant to pregnancy health.
Pregnancy can change the management of existing thyroid conditions.
Common pregnancy symptoms overlap with thyroid symptoms, so testing and professional interpretation matter.
Iodine supports thyroid hormone production, but supplementation needs individual guidance.
Medication should never be started, stopped, or changed based on app content.
Gentle takeaway: Hormone changes are part of pregnancy. If thyroid tests or medication come up in an appointment, it is a chance to ask questions — not a reason to panic.
sources: Jouanne M, et al. “Nutrient Requirements during Pregnancy and Lactation.” Discusses iodine requirements and thyroid relevance during pregnancy.
NICE. “Antenatal care: recommendations.” Supports individual assessment, medical-history review, medication review, and referral where needed.
NHS. “Vegetarian or vegan and pregnant.” Provides food and supplement-safety context relevant to iodine and B12 discussions.

lessons.title: Emotional changes during pregnancy
body: Pregnancy can bring excitement, gratitude, fear, irritation, sadness, numbness, joy, and mixed emotions — sometimes within the same day. Feeling a range of emotions does not mean someone is ungrateful for their pregnancy or incapable of becoming a good parent. It means they are moving through a major physical, emotional, social, and practical life change.

Hormone changes can affect mood, but they are not the whole story. Sleep disruption, nausea, body changes, money worries, work or school pressure, relationship changes, previous pregnancy experiences, fertility treatment, pregnancy loss, medical uncertainty, and fear of birth can all shape how a person feels.

When a pregnancy includes a suspected or confirmed Down syndrome diagnosis, uncertainty and the amount of new information can create additional emotional pressure. The St George’s NHS pathway recognises that some parents may experience difficulty bonding or coping after receiving a high-chance or confirmed diagnosis. It emphasises sensitive, non-directive, emotionally supportive care rather than assumptions about how someone should feel.

Natal IQ should reflect this approach. It should not demand positivity, pressure a user to “stay grateful,” or imply that worry is a failure. A simple daily emotional check-in can be helpful if it is framed as reflection rather than a clinical test. For example, a user could choose: calm, tired, worried, low, hopeful, overwhelmed, or mixed. The app can then offer a gentle next step — journal, grounding tool, support contact, or appointment question — rather than giving a diagnosis.
keyPoints: Mixed emotions during pregnancy are common and valid.
Emotional wellbeing is influenced by many things, not only hormones.
Feeling worried, numb, sad, or overwhelmed does not make someone a bad parent.
A suspected or confirmed diagnosis can bring specific emotional needs and deserves sensitive support.
Persistent distress, anxiety, or low mood should be discussed with a midwife, GP, mental-health professional, or trusted support service.
Gentle takeaway: You do not have to feel one “correct” way about pregnancy. Your feelings are information, and you deserve space to share them.
sources: St George’s NHS / DSRF-UK. “Personalised antenatal care of pregnancies suspected or diagnosed with Down syndrome.” Includes emotional and psychological support as a core care area.
DSRF-UK. “Pregnancy pathway.” Explains the need for tailored support for families expecting a baby with a high-chance or confirmed Down syndrome diagnosis.
PMC. “Perinatal mental health: a review of progress and challenges.” Provides research context on mental health during pregnancy and after birth.
NICE. “Antenatal care: recommendations.” Supports discussion of emotional wellbeing, social support, concerns at home, and individualised antenatal care.

lessons.title: Baby blues, depression and getting support
body: The “baby blues” are common emotional changes that can happen shortly after birth. They can include tearfulness, mood swings, irritability, anxiety, and feeling overwhelmed. These feelings often begin in the first few days after birth and usually improve within around two weeks.

Postnatal depression is different because symptoms are more persistent, intense, or disruptive. NHS information lists possible symptoms including persistent sadness or low mood, loss of interest in activities, hopelessness, guilt, anxiety, difficulty sleeping even when rest is possible, poor concentration, difficulty bonding with the baby, and thoughts of self-harm or harming the baby.

Not everyone experiences postnatal depression in the same way. Depression can also begin during pregnancy, not only after birth. Someone may feel low, irritable, anxious, detached, exhausted, frightened, or unable to enjoy things they normally would. These experiences are not evidence that they are a bad parent or that they do not love their baby.

Natal IQ should not ask a user to decide whether they “have postnatal depression.” Instead, it can say: “If these experiences sound familiar or are affecting your life, you deserve to speak with someone.” The app should provide clear support routes, such as a midwife, health visitor, GP, perinatal mental-health team, or trusted support service.

For urgent concerns — such as immediate risk of self-harm, harm to someone else, severe confusion, hallucinations, or feeling unsafe — the app must show emergency options rather than continuing with general wellbeing content.
keyPoints: Baby blues are common and usually temporary emotional changes after birth.
Persistent or severe low mood, anxiety, hopelessness, or distress can indicate a need for professional support.
Postnatal depression is treatable and does not define someone’s worth as a parent.
Difficulty bonding is a reason for support, not a reason for shame.
Urgent thoughts of self-harm or harm require immediate help.
Gentle takeaway: You do not need to wait until you are at breaking point. Support is valid the moment things feel heavier than you can carry alone.
sources: NHS. “Postnatal depression.” Primary source for postnatal-depression symptoms, treatment, and support routes.
NHS. “Your body after the birth.” Provides postnatal recovery information and emergency-care context.
Cleveland Clinic. “Postpartum: Stages, Symptoms & Recovery Time.” Covers baby blues, postpartum depression, anxiety, and psychosis.
Somerset NHS Foundation Trust. “Your emotional wellbeing and mental health.” Provides NHS maternity information on baby blues and postnatal depression.

lessons.title: Worry, anxiety and the “what-if” spiral
body: Pregnancy invites uncertainty. There are appointments, tests, changing symptoms, birth planning, work decisions, money questions, family opinions, and the huge unknown of becoming responsible for another person. Some worry is completely understandable and can even be useful when it helps someone plan or ask questions.

Anxiety can become more draining when thoughts feel constant, uncontrollable, or begin to interfere with sleep, eating, school, work, relationships, or daily functioning. Some people notice a repeated “what if?” pattern: “What if the scan finds something?” “What if I do something wrong?” “What if I cannot cope?” These thoughts can feel convincing even when they do not lead to a useful next step.

Natal IQ should not promise to eliminate anxiety. It can offer simple grounding tools and next-step prompts. A “name it” practice might help a user say, “I am having a worried thought,” rather than “this fear is definitely true.” A “small next step” tool can help users decide whether to write down a question for their next appointment, message a trusted person, take a brief pause, or contact a professional if the concern is urgent.

Research on perinatal mental health shows that anxiety and depression are common during pregnancy and after birth. It also shows that people may find it hard to disclose concerns because of stigma, fear of judgement, or worry that they will not be taken seriously. Natal IQ’s language should therefore be deliberately non-judgemental: anxiety is not attention-seeking, and reaching out is not overreacting.

For a suspected or confirmed Down syndrome diagnosis, the app should provide balanced information, links to specialist maternity support, and peer organisations. It should not frame a diagnosis as a tragedy or pressure a family toward any particular decision.
keyPoints: Worry is common during pregnancy; constant, intrusive worry deserves support.
Anxiety can affect thoughts, physical sensations, sleep, concentration, and avoidance.
Small grounding practices can help in the moment but are not substitutes for professional care.
Writing questions down can make uncertainty more manageable.
Persistent anxiety is a valid reason to contact a midwife, GP, or perinatal mental-health service.
Gentle takeaway: You do not need certainty to deserve support. If worry is taking up too much space, let someone help you carry it.
sources: PMC. “Diagnosis and management of perinatal depression and anxiety in general practice.” Reviews perinatal anxiety/depression and barriers to seeking support.
PMC. “Perinatal mental health: a review of progress and challenges.” Provides evidence context on mental health during pregnancy and the postnatal period.
PMC. “Who is actually asked about their mental health in pregnancy and the postnatal period?” Examines gaps in mental-health enquiry and support.
NHS. “Postnatal depression.” Provides user-facing support and signposting.
St George’s NHS / DSRF-UK. “Personalised antenatal care of pregnancies suspected or diagnosed with Down syndrome.” Supports sensitive, non-directive emotional care.

lessons.title: Building a support circle
body: Support is not an optional extra during pregnancy and postpartum recovery. It can affect practical wellbeing, emotional resilience, access to healthcare, and the ability to rest. Yet reaching out can be difficult. People may not want to “be a burden,” may feel awkward asking, may live far from family, or may not know what help would actually be useful.
Natal IQ’s Calm & Connect section can make asking easier by turning a vague need into a specific request. Instead of “I need help,” users could choose or adapt messages such as:
• “Could you check in with me this week?”
• “Would you be able to bring a meal on Tuesday?”
• “Can you come with me to an appointment?”
• “Could you help with school pickup or shopping after the baby arrives?”
• “I do not need advice right now — I just need someone to listen.”

The DSRF-UK pathway highlights the value of support for families expecting a baby with a high-chance or confirmed Down syndrome diagnosis and points people toward peer support services. This fits directly with Natal IQ’s purpose: being an information and connection hub, not a substitute for a clinician.

Support circles should be inclusive. A support person may be a partner, co-parent, parent, friend, sibling, neighbour, doula, social worker, faith leader, colleague, health visitor, or another parent from a peer group. Some users may not have an obvious support circle, which is why a directory of NHS services, charities, social workers, clinics, and peer communities could be valuable.

The app should also recognise boundaries. Support is not automatically helpful if it comes with criticism, pressure, or unwanted advice. Users should be able to decide what kind of contact feels safe and useful.
keyPoints: Asking for help is a practical skill, not a weakness.
Specific requests are often easier for others to respond to than vague ones.
Support can be emotional, practical, informational, or appointment-related.
Peer groups can be especially useful when friends and family do not fully understand the situation.
People deserve support that respects their decisions, culture, privacy, and boundaries.
Gentle takeaway: You do not need a huge network. One safe person, one useful contact, or one honest message can be a meaningful starting point.
sources: St George’s NHS / DSRF-UK. “Personalised antenatal care of pregnancies suspected or diagnosed with Down syndrome.” Includes emotional, psychological, antenatal, and postnatal support as core care areas.
DSRF-UK. “Pregnancy pathway.” Explains the need for tailored support for families expecting a baby with a high-chance or confirmed diagnosis.
NICE. “Antenatal care: recommendations.” Recommends discussing potential benefits of peer support and providing information about local and national peer-support services.
JMIR. “Characteristics and Quality of Mobile Apps Containing Prenatal Genetic Testing Information.” Supports the need for credible, customisable pregnancy-app information and support features.

lessons.title: Conversations with partners, co-parents and family
body: Pregnancy can change the rhythm of a relationship. One person may be physically experiencing symptoms while another feels unsure how to help. Both may have fears about money, sleep, birth, parenting, or the future. If there is a suspected or confirmed Down syndrome diagnosis, family members may also respond differently — with love, worry, silence, unwanted opinions, or uncertainty.
Natal IQ can offer communication tools without telling couples or families how they “should” run their relationship. A simple structure is:
What I feelWhat I needWhat would help

For example: “I feel overwhelmed after appointments. I need time to process. It would help if you sat with me and listened before we make decisions.” This can be clearer and less confrontational than a conversation built around blame.
Short, regular check-ins may be easier than waiting for a major argument or crisis. A weekly Calm & Connect check-in could include three questions:
• What has felt hardest this week?
• What has helped this week?
• What is one practical thing we can make easier next week?

The feature should not assume every user has a partner. Natal IQ should use inclusive language such as “partner, co-parent, family member, friend, or trusted person.” This better reflects single parents, separated parents, LGBTQ+ families, blended families, and users who do not want to involve a partner.

If a user feels controlled, frightened, isolated, threatened, or unsafe in a relationship, the app should provide a discreet pathway to specialist support. Pregnancy can be a time when domestic abuse starts or escalates. This must be handled privately and sensitively, not as a relationship-communication exercise.
keyPoints: Pregnancy can change communication and the division of responsibilities.
Specific requests are easier to hear and respond to than criticism or assumptions.
Regular short check-ins can reduce resentment and uncertainty.
Every family structure is valid; the app should not assume a partner is present.
Feeling unsafe, controlled, or frightened requires confidential professional support.
Gentle takeaway: You do not have to solve every future problem today. One honest conversation about one practical need can make the week feel lighter.
sources: NICE. “Antenatal care: recommendations.” Covers partner involvement, respectful communication, social support, and opportunities to discuss concerns at home or domestic abuse.
National Academies / NCBI Bookshelf. “Risks to Maternal Health.” Includes maternal mental-health and intimate-partner-violence context.
St George’s NHS / DSRF-UK. “Personalised antenatal care of pregnancies suspected or diagnosed with Down syndrome.” Supports sensitive, family-centred, non-directive communication.

lessons.title: Tiny calm moments that fit real life
body: Many mental-wellbeing resources recommend mindfulness, breathing, or self-care, but that can feel unrealistic when someone is nauseous, working, caring for other children, attending appointments, or running on very little sleep. Natal IQ’s approach should make calm small and accessible, not another performance task.

A “60-second reset” can be enough. The user might place both feet on the floor, notice three things they can see, take a slower breath in and out, and name one thing they need in the next hour. This does not solve every stressor. It simply creates a small pause in a tense moment.

Another option is a “permission pause”: “I can pause before replying.” Pregnancy can bring lots of opinions, messages, medical information, and family questions. A user does not have to reply immediately to messages, social-media comments, or requests for information. Giving yourself a pause can be a meaningful boundary.

The app can include short audio exercises, but they should be optional and trauma-sensitive. Some people dislike closing their eyes, focusing on their breathing, or being told to relax. Offer choices: a grounding exercise, a short walk prompt, a music break, a journal question, gentle stretching, or a message-a-friend prompt.

Mental-wellbeing support should never imply that calm breathing is a solution for depression, panic, domestic abuse, trauma, self-harm risk, or a medical emergency. It is a small supportive tool, not treatment. If a user reports feeling unsafe, unable to cope, or in crisis, the app should show urgent support contacts instead.
keyPoints: Small moments of grounding can be helpful even when there is no time for a long wellness routine.
There is no single correct way to calm down; users can choose what feels safe.
Boundaries around messages, advice, and social media are part of wellbeing.
Self-compassion can be more helpful than criticising yourself for being stressed.
Persistent distress still deserves professional support.
sources: PMC. “A Mobile App for the Self-Report of Psychological Well-Being During Pregnancy (BrightSelf).” Discusses design considerations for pregnancy wellbeing self-report apps.
PMC. “Diagnosis and management of perinatal depression and anxiety in general practice.” Reviews support needs and barriers to care.
NHS. “Postnatal depression.” Provides user-facing support and escalation information, reinforcing that self-help does not replace professional care.
PMC. “Perinatal mental health: a review of progress and challenges.” Provides wider research context on perinatal mental-health interventions and services.

extras.heading: Try this now: the 60-second reset
items: Put both feet on the floor or notice where your body is supported.
Look for three ordinary things you can see.
Let your shoulders drop if they can.
Ask: “What would make the next hour 1% easier?”
